kind: real in-game invocations of the body connectivity refresh, captured by a private bounded plugin before and after the controller listener call, compared offline with the Python chain

capture_point.reachability: 18b8860 has exactly two static call sites, both inside controller listener 18b8670 event 0; 18b8670 has no direct callers and no stored image pointer; it is reached through one row of the global body-listener registry (descriptor at image 0x33367c0) by broadcaster 18a7f60
capture_point.mechanism: registry-row callback swap (aligned 8-byte compare-exchange on heap data); no code bytes or page protections changed; detour always forwards to 18b8670
capture_point.identity_checks: image base; code fingerprints of 18b8670 (48 B), 18b8860 (32 B) and 18a7f60 (80 B); both call sites decode as call rel32 to 18b8860; exactly one enabled registry row holds 18b8670
capture_point.captured_path: event 0, metadata+0x50 bit15 clear and metadata+0x1c != controller+0x4c (the branch that stamps and calls 18b8860 without 18b8380); the priority/quiet-2 branch (18b8380 then 18b8860) is counted but not captured
capture_point.bounds: arm file written when a player body first had a controller and a +0x80 head; at most 32 captured calls; 150 s install window; per-walk caps of 6000 regions / 3 MiB; fixed 96 MiB buffer; reads via ReadProcessMemory on self; trace written by a worker thread after restore
capture_point.restore: scan the current registry for rows holding the detour and compare-exchange them back; wait for in-flight detour calls to drain; module pinned

comparison_method: expected = pre bytes + listener stamp (metadata+0x1c := pre controller+0x4c) + Python chain (analyze.run_python, recording stubs for 18e2de0, pool return and allocator); compared with post bytes the game produced at every pre-captured address. Differences are attributed to services that really ran in game (18e2de0 for processed groups/context, allocator for slot-owner vector headers, pool return for contact spans, listener enter/leave for controller+0x50..0x60); anything else is unattributed and fails the pair. Allocated vectors are compared by content at the game-installed pointer. Native 18b8860 also runs in Unicorn on the stamped pre bytes as a coverage cross-check.
verdict: PASS: 32/32 captured in-game invocations matched the Python chain on bytes not owned by in-game services (0 with nonempty +0x80 rings, 32 empty-ring early returns); 64 predicted changed bytes matched, 0 unattributed differing bytes. Across 3 sessions the hooked listener saw 10552 calls into 18b8860 and 0 via 18b8380; every one split by ring state had an empty +0x80 ring, so selection, rebuild and retire were NOT exercised by any observed in-game invocation.

overall.in_game_listener_totals_note: path_a = event 0, priority bit15 clear, stamp mismatch (stamps and calls 18b8860); path_b = priority set and quiet nibble 2 (18b8380 then 18b8860); path_none = event 0 that calls neither; gate_unreadable counts event-0 calls whose metadata/owner/controller chain was null or unreadable (the listener returns early for a null controller). path_a_nonempty_ring counts are from sessions 2-3 only (session 1 did not split them).

limits: Pre and post regions are sequential self-reads on the calling thread immediately around the listener call; other threads may run meanwhile, so the regions are not atomic snapshots.
The capture brackets the whole listener call (protected enter/leave, stamp, 18b8860, controller28 virtual+a8), not 18b8860 alone.
Services 18e2de0, pool return and the allocator ran in game; their effects are attributed by region role rather than reproduced.
Only the priority-clear stamp-mismatch branch was captured; the branch that first runs 18b8380 was not.
Native removal 18bb610 does not guard a failed search; the install window was kept short so controller teardown during the swap was not expected, but this is not excluded in general.
Session 1 (v1 plugin) captured the first 32 eligible calls, all on world bodies with empty +0x80 rings; session 2 onward filtered to nonempty rings.
Heap addresses, raw bytes and traces are private and not published.
